decisionPoints: When to treat: ONLY if causing bothersome bulge/pressure, sexual dysfunction, voiding dysfunction, or defecatory dysfunction
When surgery indicated: failed or declined pessary AND symptomatic AND desires definitive treatment
When to include apical suspension: essentially always - reduces reoperation rate
When to evaluate further for masses: if abdominal/pelvic exam suggests pathology beyond prolapse
When to assess for occult stress incontinence: before any POP surgery - may unmask with prolapse reduction
When to choose sacrocolpopexy over native tissue repair: young patient, sexually active, high-grade prolapse, prior failed vaginal surgery
When to perform supracervical vs total hysterectomy: default to supracervical unless cervical pathology or patient preference for total
When to consult urogynecology: complex mesh erosion, recurrent prolapse after sacrocolpopexy
When to reoperate for mesh erosion: symptomatic erosion, large erosion, recurrent UTIs or infections, partner dyspareunia
When to use active vs passive: Consider passive for higher first-attempt pass rate; active if concerned about occult retention
When to discharge with catheter: Failed voiding trial with PVR >150mL or >1/3 voided volume
When to consider sling loosening/revision: Persistent urinary retention despite conservative management (typically 2-4 weeks)
When to consult urogynecology: Persistent retention, suspected sling complication, recurrent UTIs with catheterization
When to perform urodynamics: unclear diagnosis, failed conservative treatment, before surgical intervention, complex presentation
When to perform cystourethroscopy: hematuria, refractory urgency, recurrent UTI, suspected fistula/foreign body
When to consider surgery: failed conservative management, patient preference after counseling, significant impact on quality of life
When to refer to urogynecology: failed first-line treatments, need for urodynamics, surgical candidate, complex/mixed incontinence
